AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: The pathogenesis of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) is characterized by the low expression of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) in airway epithelia, which decreases the production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). Conversely, cigarette smoke stimulates COX-2 expression in airway epithelia. Therefore, it was hypothesized that the development of AERD would be suppressed by elevated PGE2 levels in smokers, and smoking cessation might increase susceptibility to AERD.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: The objective of this study was to evaluate the relationship between smoking and the risk of AERD development.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: The smoking status of patients with AERD (n = 114) was compared with 2 control groups with aspirin-tolerant asthma (ATA), patients diagnosed by a systemic aspirin provocation test (ATA-1, n = 83) and outpatients randomly selected from a large-scale dataset (ATA-2, n = 914), as well as a healthy control group (HC, n = 2313).

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: At the age of asthma onset, there was a low frequency of current smokers (9.7%), but a high frequency of past smokers (20.2%) in the AERD group compared with the ATA-1 (20.5% and 12.0% for current and past smokers, respectively), ATA-2 (24.5% and 10.3%, respectively), and HC group (26.2% and 12.6%, respectively). After adjustment for confounding variables, AERD was positively associated with smoking cessation between 1 and 4 years before disease onset compared with the ATA-2 group (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.63, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.16-9.93) and the HC group (aOR 4.09, 95% CI: 2.07-8.05), implying that smoking cessation was followed by the development of AERD.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Smoking cessation may be a risk factor for the development of AERD.
